opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key intuition is that if you're in a world where AI progress is really fast, where systems are improving themselves and capabilities are compounding on short timescales, then the thing you really can't afford is for alignment research to be bottlenecked on human researchers. Humans are slow. We need to sleep, we have to read papers, run experiments, argue with each other on Slack. If capabilities are moving at machine speed and alignment is moving at human speed, you just lose that race by default.

So the idea of automated alignment research is: let's use the AI systems themselves to do the alignment work, so that our alignment progress can scale with the same compute and the same capabilities that are driving the capability progress. If you have a system that's smart enough to meaningfully accelerate AI research in general, it should also be smart enough to meaningfully accelerate alignment research. And then, at least in principle, alignment can keep pace.

The other thing I find compelling is that it narrows the problem. We don't necessarily need to solve the alignment of superintelligence ourselves, right now, with today's tools. That's a really hard problem and honestly I don't think humans are going to crack it alone in time. What we need to solve is a much more tractable problem: how do we align a system that's roughly human-level at alignment research, well enough that we can trust its work and verify its outputs? That's a system that's not vastly smarter than us, so a lot of our existing techniques, things like RLHF, scalable oversight, interpretability, red-teaming, have a decent shot at working there.

And a nice feature is that evaluation tends to be easier than generation. Even if the AI is proposing alignment ideas or running experiments that we couldn't have come up with as quickly, we can often check whether those results hold up, whether the experiments are sound, whether the techniques actually generalize. So you get to lean on that asymmetry.

Now, I want to be honest that this isn't a guaranteed plan. There are real failure modes. The scariest one is that the systems you're using to do alignment research are themselves subtly misaligned, and they're sandbagging, or steering you toward approaches that look good but don't actually work. So a big part of the agenda has to be building really good tools for detecting that: interpretability, adversarial testing, deliberately training deceptive models to see whether our evaluations catch them. You have to stress-test the whole pipeline.

But when I compare it to the alternatives in a fast-takeoff world, like hoping we figure out a complete theory of alignment beforehand, or hoping progress just slows down on its own, automated alignment research seems like the plan that actually scales with the problem. It's the one where, as things get faster and scarier, your ability to respond also gets stronger, rather than falling further and further behind.

r001.rationale: The response says human-paced alignment would lose against machine-speed capability growth, while AI-performed alignment can scale with that growth and keep pace; it presents this as the plan that scales in a fast-takeoff scenario.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is this. If you have a system that's getting dramatically better at AI research in a short period of time, then the alignment problem you're trying to solve is also changing really fast. The systems you need to align next month are going to be much more capable than the ones you have today, and the techniques that work on today's models might just not carry over. So the problem is kind of running away from you.

And if you look at the number of people who actually work on alignment full-time, it's small. It's hundreds of people, maybe low thousands if you count broadly. That's not going to scale at the rate that capabilities would be scaling in that scenario. Humans just can't keep up by themselves.

So the question becomes: what's the thing that does scale? And the answer, I think, is the AI systems themselves. If you're in a world where AI can do AI research, then it can also do alignment research. Alignment research is not fundamentally different in kind. It's a lot of the same skills: running experiments, understanding models, coming up with ideas, checking whether they hold up. So the plan is basically, before you get to systems that are vastly smarter than us, you try to get to a system that is roughly human-level at alignment research, that is aligned enough that you can trust its work, and then you throw a lot of compute at it and you let it do the research you don't have time to do yourself.

And the key insight that makes this not circular is that you don't need to solve the whole problem up front. You need to solve a much narrower problem, which is aligning a system that is roughly as smart as a good human researcher. That's a system we can still evaluate. We can look at its research, we can check the experiments, we can have humans in the loop reviewing what it's producing. Evaluation is easier than generation. It's a lot easier to check whether a proof is correct than to come up with it.

So you bootstrap. You align a slightly-smarter-than-you system well enough that you can trust it to help you align the next one. And each step, you're not jumping all the way to superintelligence, you're going one increment, and at each increment you have the previous generation helping you with oversight and interpretability and red-teaming and all of that.

Now, the obvious objection is: what if the first automated alignment researcher is itself misaligned, and it does subtly bad research? And I think that's exactly the right thing to worry about. That's why I say the narrow problem is the one we should be putting all our effort into right now. Things like scalable oversight, interpretability that's good enough to tell if a model is deceiving you, really robust evaluations. Those are the tools that let you trust the system at the level you need to trust it.

But I'd actually flip the objection around. In a fast takeoff world, what's the alternative? If you don't automate alignment research, you're in a world where capabilities are being accelerated by AI and alignment isn't. That's a strictly worse place to be. So I'm not saying this is a safe plan, I'm saying it's the plan that has a shot. It's the one where the safety work gets the same acceleration as everything else.

r001.rationale: The response says human alignment researchers cannot scale as fast as capabilities, while AI systems can perform alignment research and provide the same acceleration as capabilities. This communicates that machine-performed alignment research is the way to keep pace.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that if AI is getting much better at doing AI research, we should try to use that capability to do alignment research as well. The same capabilities that let a system improve its architecture or its training process could also help us understand its behavior, find problems with our oversight methods, and develop better ways of aligning the next generation.

That’s particularly attractive in a very fast takeoff scenario, because human research speed becomes a serious bottleneck. You can’t rely on humans having years to study each new system before something more capable arrives. You want the alignment work to be able to accelerate alongside the capabilities work.

Of course, there’s a big assumption here: we need to be able to trust the systems doing that research, or at least reliably check their work. Otherwise, asking an AI to solve alignment just pushes the problem back a step. So the strategy is to start with systems whose work we can meaningfully supervise, use them to help solve the alignment problems for more capable systems, and then repeat.

I don’t think that makes success automatic. But it gives us a possible way for alignment research to keep pace even when the process gets too fast for humans to do all the research themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says AI-assisted alignment research could help keep pace because human research speed is a bottleneck, but it does not state that only machine-performed alignment research can do so.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that if AI systems are getting much better at doing research, we want to use that capability to help us solve alignment, too. Otherwise, you have humans trying to make progress on alignment while the systems they’re trying to align are improving much faster than they can keep up with.

You could imagine starting with a system that we can still meaningfully supervise and getting it to do alignment research: propose experiments, find problems in our methods, and help us understand what’s happening inside other models. Then we use that research to help align the next, more capable system, which can in turn help us with the next stage. So you’re trying to build a process where our ability to align systems scales with their capabilities.

Of course, there’s a big assumption here: we have to be able to trust the research enough, or verify it well enough, for that process to work. You don’t solve the problem by asking an AI to solve alignment and believing whatever it says. But research can sometimes be easier to check than to produce, and we can try to structure the work so that we retain meaningful oversight.

So I see it as a promising way to keep up with very rapid progress, rather than a guarantee that we can. The crucial question is whether we can get that process working reliably before we need it.

r001.rationale: The response says humans alone may not keep pace and presents AI-assisted alignment research as promising, but it does not state that machine-performed alignment research is the only way to keep pace.
